interest: Chinese plans to revive Manchurian heavy industry after Soviet removals, and American skepticism about them.
overview: This file (893.6511, January–February 1947) documents Nationalist Chinese plans for rehabilitating the iron and steel industry in Northeast China (Manchuria) and North China, alongside American diplomatic and intelligence assessments of those proposals. It comprises a January 13, 1947 covering letter from E. A. Bayne, Special Adviser on Enemy Property Affairs in Shanghai, to James K. Penfield of the State Department's Office of Far Eastern Affairs; an enclosed technical and economic survey authored by Dr. Y. C. Sun of China's National Resources Commission (NRC) detailing 1947 production schedules across works in Anshan, Benxi, Fushun, Shijingshan, Tianjin, and Tangshan to substantiate reparations claims for Japanese industrial plants; and a February 14, 1947 critical analysis by Charles C. Stelle and Philip H. Trezise of the Division of Research for Far East (DRF). The collection illuminates the intersections of Chinese industrial ambitions, the disruptive impact of Soviet asset removals and Communist guerrilla action, Chinese hyperinflation and currency constraints, and State Department skepticism regarding Chinese production cost estimates and raw material reserves.

subfiles.about: A detailed production schedule and economic justification for reviving National Resources Commission iron and steel plants in Northeast and North China in 1947.
subfiles.from: Dr. Y. C. Sun (National Resources Commission of China)
subfiles.summary: Dr. Y. C. Sun outlines a program for the National Resources Commission to restore partial operations at key iron and steel facilities in Northeast and North China following Soviet plant removals and Communist sabotage. The plan estimates domestic demand at 200,000 tons for 1947 and sets a target to produce 190,000 tons of finished and semi-finished products, potentially saving US$ 30 million in foreign exchange. Key requirements include regular transport for raw materials, stable electric power, CNC$ 50 billion in government loans, and processing 100,000 tons of scrap metal. Crucially, the survey argues that demonstrating high technical efficiency with existing facilities will validate Chinese claims for Japanese industrial plant reparations. Detailed schedules and tables enumerate plant-by-plant capacities, monthly quotas, and chemical byproduct projections.
